newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr reverses losses in Tokyo but below 119 yen.
newsitem.headline: Dlr reverses losses in Tokyo but below 119 yen.

text.p: 0344 GMT TRADED HIGH/LOW AS OF 0600 GMT

The dollar recouped earlier losses against the yen by late Tokyo trade on Friday, helped by active U.S. fund purchases in light of the weakness of the Tokyo stock market and falling Japanese government bond yields.
The dollar rose close to the key resistance point of 119.00 yen, but rumours that the Finance Ministry had warned traders not to buy dollars above 119.00 yen capped its gains.
A Finance Ministry spokesman declined to comment on the market rumours, which temporarily pushed the dollar down to around 118.50/60 yen before it resumed rising later.
"In general principle, the ministry won't comment on rumours and movements in the market," the ministry spokesman told Reuters.

Traders had be wary of verbal intervention by the authorities to check the dollar's rise. But the fact that influential Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara will be on holiday until next Tuesday made traders less cautious about testing the dollar's topside, dealers said.
"If the U.S. jobs data tonight shows strength in the U.S. economy, that may give the geeenback a chance to reach 120 yen next week," said a senior dealer at a Japanese bank.

Economists polled by Reuters forecast on average an increase of 193,000 in July U.S. non-farm payrolls, versus a rise of 217,000 in June. The unemployment rate is seen edging down 0.1 percentage point to 4.9 percent.
The jobs data for July is due at 1230 GMT.
In sharp contrast with an upbeat U.S. economy, Japan had more weak economic data on Friday, which partly encouraged perceptions that low interest rates in Japan will continue.
Japan's domestic vehicle sales fell 10.1 percent in July from a year earlier to 471,623 units, the fourth straight month in which domestic sales had fallen on a year-on-year basis.
While Japanese exporters remained intent on selling dollars on rises, operators, notably U.S. funds, were among active buyers after the dollar fell to 118.28 yen in morning trade.

U.S. fund operators were thought to be engaged in "global carry trade" in which they raise cheap yen funds and then invest them in dollars and other assets with higher returns than in Japan. "The dollar purchases by U.S. funds may be linked to such a strategy," said a dealer at a European bank.
The Nikkei 225 suffered its sixth-largest point drop this year, ending down 527.05 points or 2.59 percent at 19,804.38. It was its first close below 20,000 since July 11.
Meanwhile, the key 182nd Japanese government bond yield fell as low as 2.085 percent, against 2.110 percent on Thursday. These factors prompted yen selling, dealers said.

Although the rising value of the dollar against the yen would boost exports from Japan and eventually rack up dollar selling pressure, operators were presently buying dollars by focusing more on the gap in economic strength between Japan and the United States than future trade problems.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reiterated his support for a strong dollar on Thursday, but also said it was "enormously" in the interests of the United States and Japan that Tokyo succeed in promoting domestic demand-led growth.
The dollar crept higher against the mark in late Tokyo, with stop-loss buying triggered at around 1.8450 marks.

A dealer at a European bank in Singapore said: "The market still wants to go long on the dollar. People are looking at 1.90 eventually." The dollar ended at 118.60/70 yen and 1.8375/85 marks in New York on Thursday. ---Tatsuo Ito in Tokyo 81-3-3432-1396/Sonali Desai in Singapore 65-8703090
